A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BEAT research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, algorithms, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions, removals, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original continuation experiments, listening studies, structural-pattern diagnostics, and ablations in Sections 4–5 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Naive Piano-Roll comparisons, POP909 evaluation, and measurements of velocity-averaging error.

M1.justification: The sparse pattern encoding, default relative pitches, mean velocities, and Transformer objective remain. However, Section 3.1 replaces fixed-grid slicing with time-signature-defined beats resampled to τ steps, while Algorithms 1–2 retain the earlier slicing procedure. The PDFs do not resolve whether this reflects an underlying method change or a revised description.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds POP909 as an unseen dataset for piano continuation, retaining the existing LMD/MuseScore coverage. The synthetic transposition task also changes its stated requirement from one semitone per bar to one semitone per beat in Section 5.2 and Appendix J.1. These are limited extensions within the existing music tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds an evaluated Naive Piano-Roll comparator. Table 3 expands the compactness comparison to CPW, AMT, and Naive Piano-Roll, although CPW and AMT already appeared in other experiments. The previous continuation and accompaniment comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix D changes the reported training budget from 30 epochs and approximately 240 GPU-hours to 50 epochs and approximately 400 GPU-hours. The transposition diagnostic is also revised from barwise to beatwise shifts. These materially change the stated experimental settings; retained numerical results do not establish whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds three substantive checks absent from v1: a dense-grid control testing the importance of sparse encoding, an out-of-distribution POP909 evaluation, and a training-data analysis quantifying information lost through velocity averaging. These extend the evidence on mechanism, generalization, and representation fidelity beyond the existing ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the listening-study standard errors, within-subject ANOVA, pairwise tests, and Holm-Bonferroni correction. No new seed counts, confidence intervals, or uncertainty procedures accompany the added benchmark results. Appendix B.2's velocity standard deviation describes within-pattern variation, not uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: New results include Naive Piano-Roll scores of 0.051/0.106/582.3 in Table 2 and POP909 FMD of 365.9 for BEAT versus 401.1–512.6 for comparators in Table 9. Table 3 adds CPW's 1215.3 compound steps, AMT's 1950.6 tokens, and Naive Piano-Roll's 29340.9 tokens. Appendix B.2 reports exact velocity preservation for 99.5% of active patterns. Appendix A.2 adds an unquantified observation favoring absolute pitches with limited data. Existing numerical entries and main result plots are retained.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix B revise the formal setup: N is no longer defined there as ceil(T/τ), and τ specifies resampled slots within musically defined beats. The earlier relation nevertheless remains in the pseudocode. Base-3 encoding, pitch-offset equations, and complexity statements are retained; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows compactness superiority from existing methods generally to basic event- and notation-based tokenizations, and replaces human-like variation with balanced variation tied to specific evidence. The conclusion removes the claim of unifying previously incompatible advantages. The abstract and central musical-quality and controllability contributions remain.

C2.justification: New Section 6 specifies limits involving unquantized performance MIDI, vocabulary growth, velocity detail, and pitch-encoding generality. Appendix A recasts relative pitch encoding as optional, treats ascending and descending orders as largely interchangeable, and explains larger temporal steps through sparse training of rare patterns. New analyses also support interpretations about encoding-specific gains, generalization, and near-lossless velocity averaging.

D1.justification: v2 adds source-code access instructions, dense-baseline implementation details, explicit absolute pitch encoding for synthetic diagnostics, fuller synthetic-data construction, and clarification of the 24 scales used for SC. It revises reported training resources. Conversely, it removes decoder Algorithm 3, the exact processed-dataset statistics table, and the MuseScore collection-method link. These substantially alter reproducibility documentation without establishing corresponding implementation changes.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 add discussion of MusicVAE, Measure by Measure, Music Transformer, and streaming audio accompaniment. New Appendix K expands background with MidiNet, MuseGAN, and MidiTok, and POP909 gains a dataset citation. This broadens context while retaining the central positioning around sparse grid tokenization for autoregressive models.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to the framework explanation, diagnostic motivation, ablation discussion, and conclusion; adds limitations and background sections; and updates affiliations and publication information. Existing appendices are renumbered around additions. The overall narrative and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 gain rows, a POP909 table is added, and the dataset-count table and decoding algorithm display are removed. Figures 6–8 use replacement score illustrations, Figure 3 gains a more explanatory caption, and several displays move. The main plots, visual style, and overall layout remain largely unchanged.

improvement.justification: The grid control, POP909 evaluation, and velocity-error measurements address specific evidence gaps in v1, while explicit limitations and narrower claims improve interpretation. The gain is limited by unresolved discrepancies between revised method prose and retained pseudocode, unchanged scores despite revised training/task descriptions, and removal of standalone decoding and exact dataset documentation. Overall, v2 provides useful additional support and qualification without resolving all reproducibility ambiguities.
